children: Robots are not about to hollow out the workforce, Apollo's chief economist Torsten Slok argued.

A new Anthropic paper estimates that present-day machines could substitute for roughly 300,000 jobs in an economy that employs about 160 million people. Slok stated that even under aggressive assumptions, broad displacement of physical labor would take decades. Historical rates of cost decline imply it would take about 40 years for robots to reach cost parity on just 10% of jobs.

The gap is widest where the work looks ordinary from a distance. Nursing, general repair, an electrician threading cable through a finished wall, and a home health aide lifting a frail patient remain close to out of reach. Present robots can do almost none of that work. Most jobs are bundles of simple and complicated tasks, so a machine that handles the easy slice still cannot do the job. The mess is the moat.

Much of the automation arriving this decade also has little to do with large language models. Vehicle-scanning car washes, warehouse sortation lines, and autonomous vehicles descend from sensing and control systems that were already advancing before the current AI boom and would likely have arrived anyway. The hardest physical work is harder to automate than the consensus assumes, and the gains that do materialize will owe more to decades of mechanical engineering than to this moment in software.

For investors, the implication is modest job loss, held back by cost, fine manipulation robots still cannot manage, regulation, and a preference for human hands. Displacement is only one side of the ledger. U.S. business formation is at a record, and new firms are where new jobs come from. The net effect on employment is likely to be positive by a wide margin. Very few jobs are a single automatable task.
